html:
The Tunisian Constitution of 1861 was the first written constitution in the Arab and Muslim world. It was granted by Muhammad al-Sadiq Bey, the ruler of Tunis, under the Ottoman sultan.

It followed the Fundamental Pact of 1857, which promised equal rights and security to all subjects, including Jews and foreigners. The constitution set up a Grand Council to share power with the bey and limited his right to spend public money. Reformers such as Khayr al-Din pushed for it, as did European consuls.

It lasted only three years. A revolt against higher taxes in 1864 led the bey to suspend it. Debts to European bankers grew, and in 1881 France took over by the Treaty of Bardo. Tunisians still count it as an early start of their constitutional tradition, after the earlier abolition of slavery in 1846. See also Tunisia.
sum: The Tunisian Constitution of 1861 was the first written constitution in the Arab and Muslim world. It was granted by Muhammad al-Sadiq Bey, the ruler of Tunis, under the Ottoman sultan.
